title: New Product Design & Development
summary: The structured NPD workflow: voice of customer, concept generation, DFM/DFA, prototyping, and design reviews.

infobox.title: NPD Quick Specs
infobox.primaryFields: Product Development, Manufacturing, Quality, Project Management

sections.heading: What Is New Product Development?
sections.content: **New Product Development (NPD)** is the end-to-end process of turning a market need into a manufacturable, sellable product. It spans idea generation, engineering design, validation, and launch. A disciplined NPD process is what separates products that ship on time and budget from projects that stall in engineering change loops.

sections.heading: The Stage-Gate Process
sections.content:
The **Stage-Gate** model breaks product development into phases separated by decision gates:

1. **Discovery & Ideation** — market research, technology scouting
2. **Scoping** — feasibility study, business case
3. **Concept Development** — requirements and design concepts
4. **Detail Design & Engineering** — CAD, analysis, drawings
5. **Prototyping & Testing** — validation against requirements
6. **Production Ramp-up & Launch** — tooling, process validation

Each **gate** is a go / no-go / rework decision. Gates prevent early design errors from becoming expensive late-stage rework — the single most effective cost control in product development.

sections.heading: Requirements: Voice of the Customer
sections.content:
Every successful product starts with a quantified requirements list, not an intuition. Capture the **Voice of the Customer (VOC)** through interviews, surveys, and field data, then translate qualitative needs into measurable engineering targets using **QFD (Quality Function Deployment)** — the "house of quality."

Good requirements are **SMART**: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Example: *"the handle shall transmit 500 N of pull force for 10,000 cycles without permanent deformation"* — not *"the handle should be strong."*

sections.heading: Concept Generation & Selection
sections.content:
Generate multiple solutions before committing to one. Structured methods include:

- **Morphological analysis** — combine sub-solutions per function into a solution matrix
- **TRIZ** — resolve contradictions using known inventive principles
- **Benchmarking** — reverse-engineer competitive solutions
- **Brainstorming / 6-3-5** — rapid idea volume, judge later

Score concepts against a **weighted decision matrix** (criteria like cost, performance, risk, manufacturability, serviceability) before detail design begins. A down-selected, documented concept is the cleanest way to kill expensive dead-ends early.

sections.heading: Design for Manufacturing & Assembly (DFM/DFA)
sections.content:
**DFM** (Design for Manufacturing) simplifies the design so parts are easy and cheap to produce with available processes. **DFA** (Design for Assembly) minimizes assembly effort. Key rules:

- Minimize the **number of parts** — combine functions into one part
- Design parts that **self-locate and self-align** during assembly
- Use **symmetrical or obviously asymmetrical** parts to prevent misfeeding
- Reduce **fastener types** — standardize screws, clips, snap-fits
- Favor **standard stock sizes** and common tolerances for machined features

DFA efficiency quantifies the result:

$$E_{DFA} = \frac{3 \times N_{min}}{T_{assembly}} \times 100\%$$

where $N_{min}$ is the theoretical minimum number of parts and $T_{assembly}$ is the total manual assembly time in seconds. **Boothroyd-Dewhurst DFA** is the industry-standard methodology for this calculation.

sections.heading: Prototyping & Validation
sections.content:
Prototypes de-risk the design before tooling investment:

- **Conceptual prototypes** — 3D-printed or foam models to explore form and fit
- **Functional prototypes** — machined or SLA parts for mechanical testing
- **Engineering samples** — near-production parts to validate process capability
- **Pilot production** — first articles from production tooling

Couple physical testing with [[cae-analysis|CAE simulation]] so each prototype cycle is guided by predicted behavior rather than trial and error.

sections.heading: Design Reviews & FMEA
sections.content:
**Formal design reviews** at each development phase bring fresh eyes onto the design. A structured **Design FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis)** identifies how the product could fail, rates Severity × Occurrence × Detection, and drives corrective actions *before* release.

| FMEA Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Failure Mode | How the part could fail (e.g., fatigue crack) |
| Severity (S) | How bad the failure is (1-10) |
| Occurrence (O) | How likely it is (1-10) |
| Detection (D) | How likely inspection misses it (1-10) |
| RPN | Risk Priority Number = S × O × D |

Attack the highest RPN items first. A completed FMEA also becomes the basis for test plans and quality control documentation.

sections.heading: The Digital Thread: CAD → CAE → CAM
sections.content:
Modern NPD runs on a **digital thread** — one continuous data flow across tools:

- [[cad-computer-aided-design|CAD]] — the master 3D model and drawings
- [[cae-analysis|CAE]] — stress, thermal, and dynamic validation of the geometry
- [[cam-computer-aided-manufacturing|CAM]] — toolpaths and CNC programs from the same geometry
- [[gdnt-fundamentals|GD&T]] — the tolerancing language carried on drawings to inspection

When the model is the single source of truth, engineering changes propagate instantly instead of requiring manual redraws — the foundation of faster, cheaper, higher-quality launches.

keyTakeaways: Stage-Gate development with explicit go/no-go gates is the most reliable route to on-time, on-budget launches.
Quantified requirements (VOC/QFD) prevent subjective design drift.
DFM/DFA applied early typically cuts manufacturing cost by 30-50%.
Design FMEA prioritizes risk with RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection.
A CAD → CAE → CAM digital thread keeps the model as the single source of truth.
